items.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018
items.q: And two guys from Blood, Sweat & Tears, Lew Soloff, who you’ll probably mention later, and Alan Rubin

ctx.x: Was there an aha moment or an epiphany or something along the way that caused you do get better like that?

Not get better, but two things that I’m going to mention at this clinic I’m doing for mostly rock & rollers, a couple of jazzers, this Friday, a couple of days from now, in Northampton, that I had mentioned to you. I was asked to do a clinic. So I’m going to talk about “Spinning Wheel” and the importance of an arrangement to make good music. That’s a good question. I’m forgetting your question. Oh an aha moment. First of all, when I was a little kid I remember being in the crib, I’m the middle kid, and my mother…
Oh it was in the lease.

items.title: Lew Soloff interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000
items.q: Whereas what I’m saying is the real creative forces in that band was a particular arranger to me named Lipsius.

ctx.x: Well let’s put it this way. Marriage is not an easy thing for people, to live together for years. And married people usually the husband goes out and he’s working all day and in today’s world sometimes the wife too. And you only see each other for a few hours at night and a few hours in the morning. When you’re in a band and you’re on the road, you are with these guys night and day, four or five days a week. And when you take a trip you’re with them night and day seven days a week, except when you’re sleeping. So…

same tunes over and over again, becoming prisoners of our own hits. Whereas what I’m saying is the real creative forces in that band was a particular arranger to me named Lipsius. I mean Halligan also, but Lipsius was the prime creative arranger in the band. And he is kind of a shy, laid back sort. And oh man, he would bring in this chart or that chart and instead of saying okay we’ll do this, okay we’ll record this, it was like naaa that’s no good, naaa that’s no good. And finally he just stopped.
Yeah, he had less arrangements on those records than he should have.
